brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: According to the course, what are the two axes that form the foundation of the Social Style framework?
choices: Introversion vs. Extroversion and Thinking vs. Feeling
Tell vs. Ask (X-axis) and Task vs. People (Y-axis)
Speed vs. Accuracy and Emotion vs. Logic
Confidence vs. Humility and Direction vs. Support
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the two-axis framework is built on how someone communicates (tell or ask) and what drives them (tasks or people).
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework uses observable communication behavior, not personality psychology. The two axes are Tell vs. Ask on the X-axis and Task vs. People focus on the Y-axis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a signature question most likely asked by a Driver?
choices: How does this work and how was it measured?
Why should we choose this solution and why now?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Who else is using this and who should be involved?
questions.feedback_correct: Drivers lead with "What?"—they want to know outcomes and results right away.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember: Drivers ask "What?", Analyticals ask "How?", Amiables ask "Why?", and Expressives ask "Who?". The Driver's focus on results and outcomes drives their signature question.

questions.question: What do Analytical and Driver styles share in common?
choices: Both show high levels of visible emotion in conversations
Both tend to tell rather than ask for what they want
Both are focused on tasks and outcomes rather than relationships
Both prefer storytelling and vision-focused discussions
questions.feedback_correct: Both Drivers and Analyticals share a task focus—what separates them is that Drivers tell while Analyticals ask.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The key shared trait between Driver and Analytical is their task focus. The difference is in their communication style: Drivers tell and decide fast, while Analyticals ask many questions and move methodically.

questions.question: What does the course identify as the primary indicator that a pressure behavior is occurring?
choices: The customer begins asking for a discount on your offer
The customer has stopped listening and is checking their phone
The conversation is taking longer than expected to conclude
The customer shows a signature behavior like pulling back, going quiet, or becoming argumentative
questions.feedback_correct: Pressure behaviors are the specific observable reactions each style has when something goes wrong—they signal that your approach needs adjustment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Pressure behaviors are not just delays or distractions—they are specific style-driven responses like a Driver taking control, an Analytical asking for more time, an Expressive becoming argumentative, or an Amiable withdrawing.

questions.question: When selling to an Amiable customer, which of these tactics is most important to establish first?
choices: Lead immediately with data and evidence to build credibility
Give them clear options and specific next steps to keep control of the sale
Spend real time on rapport and explain how you arrived at this meeting
Ask ambitious vision questions and let them lead the conversation
questions.feedback_correct: Amiables prioritize relationships and safety, so building genuine rapport before business talk is essential to their buying process.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Amiables need to feel safe and connected before engaging on business matters. Jumping straight to data or rushing decisions will create distance rather than trust with this style.

questions.question: What does the course mean by "adjacent style," and why does it matter in reading a customer?
choices: It is a secondary style that sits next to the primary style on the grid and softens or modifies how the primary style shows up
It is a completely different style a customer adopts when they feel pressured or defensive
It is the style a customer would be if they were more mature or experienced in their role
It is a backup style that only shows up when the customer is communicating via email instead of in person
questions.feedback_correct: The adjacent style explains mixed signals—it's why a Driver might seem warmer than expected or an Amiable more assertive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The adjacent style is not a defense mechanism or a situational switch. It is a neighboring style on the grid that influences how someone's primary style is expressed in everyday behavior.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the primary difference between how you should prepare for an Analytical versus how you should prepare for a Driver?
choices: Analyticals want detailed evidence and time to evaluate; Drivers want speed, conclusions first, and clear options to choose from
Analyticals prefer storytelling and big-picture vision; Drivers want small talk and relationship building before business
Drivers need lots of data and proof; Analyticals want to move fast and get straight to the point
Both styles require the same preparation; the only difference is how much emotion you show during the meeting
questions.feedback_correct: This reflects the core difference between task-focused styles: Drivers are efficiency-driven and time-sensitive, while Analyticals are rigor-driven and need thorough evaluation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The preparation approaches are quite different. Drivers are impatient with process; Analyticals respect detailed process. Leading with conclusions works for Drivers but not Analyticals, who need to see the evidence trail.

questions.question: What does the course teach about the relationship between a sales rep's own Social Style and their effectiveness with different customer types?
choices: Your own style does not matter as long as you know the customer's style
Your natural style works equally well with all customer types regardless of differences
Your own defaults shape how your approach lands, and you must be aware of this to adjust and build versatility
You should completely abandon your natural style and adopt the customer's style instead
questions.feedback_correct: Awareness of your own style and defaults is step one to versatility—you cannot adjust if you do not know what you naturally do.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Your style matters because your natural approach (pace, emotion, directness) will land differently with different customers. Recognizing this is how you build the discipline to adjust and remove friction.

questions.question: Based on the framework, if a customer suddenly gives shorter answers, breaks eye contact, and shifts their body language, what should you interpret this as?
choices: A sign that the customer is no longer interested in your product and you should move toward closing
An early warning signal of a style mismatch that gives you time to identify and correct your approach
A normal part of the sales process and not necessarily a concern
Evidence that the customer's adjacent style is showing and you need to wait for their primary style to return
questions.feedback_correct: Sudden drops in engagement are early warning signs—catching them means you can still shift and recover rapport before trust is seriously damaged.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A drop in engagement is not just background noise in a meeting—it is a signal that something in your approach has created distance. The earlier you catch it, the easier it is to recover.

questions.question: What is the most important practical takeaway the course offers for using the Social Style framework in your next sales call?
choices: Perfect your presentation deck so it appeals to all four styles equally
Identify the customer's style before you pitch, listen for their signature question, and adjust your approach accordingly
Learn to recognize pressure behaviors so you can end the call gracefully if the customer becomes difficult
Know your own style so well that you can predict exactly how the customer will react to everything you say
questions.feedback_correct: This is the operational core of the framework—read, name, adjust—applied in real time in your next conversation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework is built for action, not perfection. The next step is to observe in the first few minutes, identify the style, and make one deliberate adjustment before you pitch.
